tagline: A prophet told to marry an unfaithful wife becomes the living picture of God's wounded, relentless covenant love for a people who have gone after other gods.
overview:
Hosea is the first of the twelve shorter prophetic books that close the Old Testament, and it opens with one of the strangest commands in Scripture. God tells the prophet to marry a woman who will be unfaithful to him and to give their children names that announce judgment: Jezreel, No Compassion, and Not My People. Hosea's marriage to Gomer becomes a sermon lived out in a household. As she leaves him for other lovers, Israel has left the LORD for Baal, the storm and fertility god of Canaan, and for the protection of foreign empires. And as Hosea is told to go and love her again, the LORD declares that he will not finally give up his people.

The rest of the book (chapters 4 to 14) is a collection of oracles, dense, compressed, and often abrupt, spoken to the northern kingdom of Israel in its last decades. Hosea indicts priests who have stopped teaching, kings who come and go by assassination, a people who worship calf images at Bethel and Samaria, and politicians who run to Egypt one year and Assyria the next. He calls it adultery. Yet the same book contains some of the most tender speech God makes anywhere in the Bible: the Father who taught his child to walk (11:3), the husband who will speak tenderly to his wife in the wilderness (2:14), the God who cries, “How could I give you up, O Ephraim?” (11:8).

Hosea matters because it gave Israel, and later the church, its deepest language for what sin is and what love is. Sin is not only lawbreaking; it is betrayal of a person. God's love is not sentiment; it is covenant faithfulness that grieves, judges, and pursues. Jesus twice quoted Hosea's “I desire mercy, not sacrifice” (6:6), Matthew heard Israel's story fulfilled in the child Jesus (11:1), and Paul used the renaming of Not My People to describe Gentiles welcomed into God's family (Romans 9:25-26).
author:
The book names its prophet as Hosea son of Beeri (1:1) and tells us almost nothing else about him apart from his marriage. His name comes from the same Hebrew root as Joshua and Jesus and means something like salvation or the LORD saves. He was almost certainly a native of the northern kingdom: he speaks of Israel's kings as our king (7:5), knows the towns and shrines of the north intimately, and writes Hebrew with features many scholars regard as northern. Among the writing prophets he is the one who addressed the northern kingdom as his own people; Amos, his near contemporary, was a Judean who preached in the north.

Tradition holds that the book preserves Hosea's own words, and the first-person account in chapter 3 reads like his testimony. Most scholars, including many conservative ones, think the oracles were collected and arranged by Hosea's disciples, and that the book was carried south to Judah after Samaria fell in 722 BC. Critical scholars often assign some passages, especially the references to Judah and a number of the promises of restoration, to later Judean editors who applied Hosea's message to their own kingdom. Others argue that Hosea himself addressed Judah and spoke of hope, since both judgment and restoration run through the book from its first chapter.
date:
The superscription (1:1) dates Hosea's ministry to the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah in Judah, and of Jeroboam II in Israel. That places its beginning before Jeroboam's death, around 753 BC, and suggests it lasted several decades, into the 720s. The oracles reflect the prosperity of Jeroboam's reign (chapter 2), the chaos of the years after it, when kings were murdered one after another (7:7; 8:4), and the pressure of the Assyrian empire under Tiglath-pileser III, who began to rule in 745 BC (5:13; 7:11; 8:9). Many scholars connect 5:8-15 with the Syro-Ephraimite war of about 734 to 732 BC.

The book never clearly describes the fall of Samaria in 722 BC as past, and scholars differ on whether Hosea lived to see it. Most date his active preaching from about 755 to about 725 BC, with the book reaching its final form later in Judah. Those who see extensive Judean editing date parts of the book to the seventh or sixth century BC.
setting:
Hosea spoke to the northern kingdom, which he often calls Ephraim after its largest tribe, or Samaria after its capital. When he began, Israel was enjoying the long reign of Jeroboam II (roughly the first half of the eighth century BC), a time of territorial expansion, trade, and wealth for those at the top, while Assyria was temporarily weak. The wealth did not produce faithfulness. Worship of the LORD at royal shrines like Bethel, where Jeroboam I had set up a golden calf nearly two centuries earlier (1 Kings 12:28-29), had blurred into the worship of Baal, the Canaanite god believed to send rain and fertility.

After Jeroboam II died, the kingdom collapsed from within. Of the six kings who followed him, four were assassinated (Zechariah, Shallum, Pekahiah, and Pekah), as 2 Kings 15 records. Assyria revived under Tiglath-pileser III, and Israel's rulers lurched between paying tribute to Assyria and seeking help from Egypt. Menahem paid Assyria a heavy tribute (2 Kings 15:19-20). Pekah joined Damascus against Assyria and against Judah, and lost Galilee and Gilead in about 733 to 732 BC. The last king, Hoshea, withheld tribute and turned to Egypt (2 Kings 17:4); the Assyrians besieged Samaria for three years, and it fell in 722 BC. Much of its population was deported, and the northern kingdom never returned. Hosea's first hearers lived in that downward spiral.
purpose:
Hosea was sent to call Israel back to the LORD before it was too late, and to explain, when it was too late, why judgment had come. The book names the nation's sin with unusual precision: worship of Baal and of calf images, a priesthood that had stopped teaching God's law, political alliances that put trust in empires, and a society full of lying, murder, and theft. It traces all of it to one root, the lack of knowledge of God (4:1, 6), meaning not information but the loyal, intimate relationship of a covenant partner.

The book was also preserved for later readers. In Judah it warned a southern kingdom tempted by the same sins, and after the exile it gave hope that the God who judged would also heal. Its closing verse addresses every future reader directly: whoever is wise should understand these things (14:9).
story:
Hosea stands near the end of the northern kingdom's story, which began when ten tribes broke away from David's house after Solomon's death (1 Kings 12). It builds on the exodus, the wilderness, and the covenant at Sinai, all of which Hosea recalls as Israel's youth and first love (2:15; 11:1; 13:4-5). It shares the historical world of 2 Kings 14 to 17, and it overlaps with the ministries of Amos in the north and Isaiah and Micah in the south.

The fall of Samaria in 722 BC, which Hosea foresaw, is the first of the Bible's two great exiles; Judah's exile to Babylon followed in 587 or 586 BC. Hosea's picture of Israel as God's unfaithful wife shaped later prophets, especially Jeremiah (Jeremiah 2 to 3) and Ezekiel (Ezekiel 16 and 23), and his promises of a renewed covenant, a return, and a king from David's line (3:5) point forward to the restoration the rest of the Bible anticipates.
christ:
Hosea points to Christ in several ways, some direct and some by pattern. The promise that Israel will seek the LORD and David their king in the last days (3:5) belongs to the Old Testament hope for a king from David's line, which the New Testament sees fulfilled in Jesus. Matthew cites “out of Egypt I called My son” (11:1) when the child Jesus returns from Egypt (Matthew 2:15); Hosea was speaking of the exodus, and Matthew presents Jesus as the true Son who relives Israel's story faithfully. Paul and Peter read the renaming of Not My People as God's mercy reaching the Gentiles (Romans 9:25-26; 1 Peter 2:10).

Jesus himself used Hosea 6:6 to rebuke religion without mercy (Matthew 9:13; 12:7). Many Christians hear the promise of being raised up on the third day (6:2) behind the early confession that Christ was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:4), though the New Testament never quotes the verse directly. Paul turns the taunt at death in 13:14 into a song of resurrection victory (1 Corinthians 15:55). Above all, Hosea's marriage anticipates the New Testament picture of Christ as a husband who gives himself for an unfaithful bride to make her his own (Ephesians 5:25-27).
reading:
Hosea is poetry, and hard poetry. Its Hebrew is among the most difficult in the Old Testament, and translations differ more here than in most books, so a note that says the Hebrew is uncertain is telling the truth. The oracles jump between speakers, between Israel and Judah, and between judgment and hope, often without warning. Read in short units, notice who is speaking, and let the images do their work: a half-baked cake, a senseless dove, a morning mist, a stubborn heifer, a lion, a moth.

The marriage metaphor is the key to the book and needs care. It uses the social world of ancient Israel, in which a husband held legal authority over his wife, and some of its images of punishment (especially in chapter 2) are harsh and disturbing to modern readers. The metaphor describes God's relationship with a nation, not a model for human marriages, and it has been wrongly used to excuse the abuse of women. Read it as it was meant, as the language of betrayed covenant love, and watch where it goes: every speech of judgment in chapters 1 to 3 ends in a promise of renewal. Finally, Hosea uses several names for the same people: Israel, Ephraim, Samaria, and Jacob usually all mean the northern kingdom.

structure.title: Hosea's marriage and the LORD's marriage
structure.summary: Hosea marries Gomer, and their children's names announce judgment. The LORD indicts unfaithful Israel as a wife gone after Baal, then promises to woo her back. Hosea buys back his wife, a picture of Israel's discipline and return.

structure.title: No knowledge of God in the land
structure.summary: The LORD brings charges against Israel: faithless priests, idolatry, sexual immorality at the shrines, and rulers who run to Assyria. A call to return (6:1-3) is answered by a God who finds their loyalty as short-lived as morning mist.

structure.title: Sowing the wind
structure.summary: Kings made without God, calf images, foreign alliances, and empty festivals will bring invasion and exile. Israel's history of sin, from Baal-peor to Gibeah, will be repaid.

structure.title: The Father's love
structure.summary: God remembers calling his son out of Egypt and teaching him to walk. Though Israel will go into exile, God refuses to destroy him completely and promises a return.

structure.title: From Jacob to the final call
structure.summary: Israel's deceit is traced back to its ancestor Jacob, and its idolatry to forgetting the God of the exodus. After a final announcement of death, the book closes with an invitation to return and God's promise to heal and love freely.

themes.title: Covenant love (hesed)
themes.body: Hosea's key word is hesed, rendered in the BSB as loving devotion or loyalty. It names the steadfast faithfulness that partners in a covenant owe one another, love expressed in loyalty. God has shown it to Israel from the exodus onward; Israel's hesed toward God is like morning dew that vanishes (6:4). God wants it more than sacrifice (6:6), and in the end he will betroth his people to himself in it (2:19).

themes.title: Idolatry as adultery
themes.body: Hosea is the first prophet to develop at length the picture of Israel as the LORD's wife and idolatry as unfaithfulness. The image is not decorative. It says that worship is a relationship of exclusive loyalty, that turning to Baal or to empires for security is betrayal, and that God's anger is the anger of a wounded husband, not a bureaucrat. The same picture carries the hope of reconciliation.

themes.title: The knowledge of God
themes.body: The charge that there is no knowledge of God in the land (4:1) runs through the book. In Hebrew, to know can describe intimate relationship, including marriage, and to know God means to acknowledge him, trust him, and live by his instruction. The priests have rejected knowledge (4:6), and the promised future is that Israel will know the LORD (2:20).

themes.title: Politics and false security
themes.body: Hosea treats Israel's foreign policy as a spiritual matter. Kings are made without consulting God (8:4), and envoys run between Egypt and Assyria like a senseless dove (7:11). Trust in armies, alliances, and fortified cities is another form of idolatry, and it will fail.

themes.title: Judgment and return
themes.body: The Hebrew verb shuv, to turn or return, sounds throughout Hosea. Israel will not return to God, so God will return them to a new Egypt in exile. Yet the book ends with God's own call to return and his promise to heal their apostasy and love them freely (14:1-4). Judgment is real, but it is not the last word.

keyChapters.why: The command to marry Gomer and the naming of the children set out the whole book's message of judgment and reversal.
The LORD's case against his unfaithful wife ends with the promise to lead her into the wilderness, speak tenderly to her, and betroth her forever.
Hosea buys back his wife, the book's clearest picture of costly, disciplined, restoring love.
A call to return, the complaint that Israel's loyalty is like morning mist, and the verse Jesus quoted: God desires mercy, not sacrifice.
God as the Father who taught Israel to walk, and whose compassion will not let him destroy his son.
The closing invitation to return and God's promise to heal and love freely.

parts.body:
Hosea is the first of the twelve shorter prophets that close the Old Testament. It has 14 chapters. Hosea son of Beeri spoke to the northern kingdom of Israel in its last decades, from the good years of Jeroboam II, before about 753 BC, into the years when Assyria swallowed it.

The book opens with a command that still startles readers. God tells Hosea to marry a woman who will be unfaithful, ‘because this land is flagrantly prostituting itself by departing from the LORD’ (1:2). Hosea marries Gomer, and their three children are given names that announce judgment: Jezreel, No Compassion, and Not My People. His broken home becomes a sermon. Israel has left the LORD for Baal, the rain and fertility god of Canaan, and for the protection of empires.

Chapters 4 to 14 are short, sharp oracles. Hosea charges the priests, the kings and the people with forgetting God. They make kings without him, bow to calf images, and run between Egypt and Assyria. He calls it adultery, and he warns that it will end in exile.

Yet this same book holds some of the tenderest words God speaks anywhere. He will lead his people into the wilderness and ‘speak to her tenderly’ (2:14). He taught Ephraim to walk (11:3). He cries, ‘How could I give you up, O Ephraim?’ (11:8). The book ends with words for the people to pray and God's answer, ‘I will heal their apostasy; I will freely love them’ (14:4).

parts.h: Where it sits in the story
parts.body:
Hosea stands near the end of the northern kingdom's story. Ten tribes broke away from David's house after Solomon died (1 Kings 12), and their first king, Jeroboam I, set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan so that his people would not go up to Jerusalem to worship. Two centuries later Hosea is still speaking against the calf of Samaria.

The book shares its world with 2 Kings 14 to 17, which tells the same years from the throne. Amos, a man from Judah, preached in the north at about the same time, and Isaiah and Micah preached in Judah. Hosea is the one writing prophet who addressed the northern kingdom as his own people.

He reaches back as well as forward. He recalls Jacob, the nation's ancestor (chapter 12), the exodus, the wilderness and Israel's youth (2:15; 11:1; 13:4-5), and the sin at Baal-peor in the wilderness (9:10). He looks ahead to the fall of Samaria, the first of the Bible's two great exiles, and past it to a return. His picture of Israel as the LORD's unfaithful wife shaped Jeremiah (Jeremiah 2 to 3) and Ezekiel (Ezekiel 16 and 23).

The book names its prophet as Hosea son of Beeri (1:1) and tells almost nothing else about him apart from his marriage. His name comes from the same Hebrew root as Joshua and means something like salvation. He was almost certainly from the north. He speaks of the king in Samaria as his own people's king (7:5), he knows the northern towns and shrines closely, and many scholars hear northern features in his Hebrew.

Tradition holds that the book keeps Hosea's own words, and chapter 3, told in the first person, reads like his own account. Most scholars, many conservative ones among them, think his disciples collected and arranged the oracles, and that the book was carried south to Judah after Samaria fell. Critical scholars often give some passages, especially those that mention Judah and some of the promises of restoration, to later editors in Judah. Others answer that Hosea himself spoke to Judah and spoke of hope, since judgment and restoration run through the book from its first chapter.

The heading dates Hosea by four kings of Judah, from Uzziah to Hezekiah, and one king of Israel, Jeroboam II (1:1). So he began before Jeroboam died, about 753 BC, and went on for decades. The dates given on this site differ a little. The site's guide to the kings gives about 755 to 715 BC. The book's own introduction gives about 755 to about 725, and says scholars differ on whether Hosea lived to see Samaria fall, since the book never clearly describes it as past.

When Hosea began, Israel was enjoying the long reign of Jeroboam II, a time of wider borders, trade and wealth for those at the top, while Assyria was weak for a time. The wealth did not make the people faithful. Worship at the royal shrines, like Bethel, had blurred into the worship of Baal, the god many believed sent rain and good harvests. The site's notes on chapter 2 point to eighth-century receipts found at Samaria that include personal names built on Baal beside names built on the LORD's name.

After Jeroboam died, the kingdom came apart from within. Of the six kings who followed him, four were assassinated: Zechariah, Shallum, Pekahiah and Pekah (2 Kings 15). Assyria revived under Tiglath-pileser III, who began to rule in 745 BC. Israel's rulers swung between paying tribute to Assyria and asking Egypt for help. Menahem paid Assyria a heavy tribute (2 Kings 15:19-20). Pekah joined Damascus against Assyria and lost Galilee and Gilead in about 733 to 732 BC. Many scholars connect 5:8-15 with that war. The last king, Hoshea, stopped paying and turned to Egypt (2 Kings 17:4). Assyria besieged Samaria for three years, and it fell. The book's introduction gives 722 BC; the guide to the kings, following Thiele's dates, gives 723 or 722.

Hosea's first hearers lived in that downward spiral. His words about kings made ‘not by Me’ (8:4) and about a ‘silly, senseless dove’ (7:11) are about real kings and real envoys.

The book has two unequal parts. Chapters 1 to 3 tell of Hosea's marriage and set it beside the LORD's marriage to Israel: the children named in judgment (chapter 1), the LORD's case against his unfaithful wife and his promise to win her back (chapter 2), and Hosea buying back his wife (chapter 3). Each of these three chapters moves from judgment to hope.

Chapters 4 to 14 are collected oracles, dense and often abrupt. They can be read in three movements, each ending in hope. Chapters 4 to 7 bring the charge that there is no knowledge of God in the land. Chapters 8 to 11 warn that those who sow the wind will reap the whirlwind, and end with the Father who will not give up his son. Chapters 12 to 14 trace Israel's deceit back to Jacob and end with the last call to return.

Hosea is poetry, and its Hebrew is among the hardest in the Old Testament. Translations differ here more than in most books, and the notes say so where the Hebrew is uncertain. The speaker changes without warning, and so does the subject, from Israel to Judah and from judgment to hope. Hosea also uses several names for the same people. Israel, Ephraim, Samaria and Jacob usually all mean the northern kingdom.

‘Go, take a prostitute as your wife and have children of adultery’ (1:2). Readers have always been troubled by this command, and the book's notes set out the main readings without choosing between them. Some think Gomer was already known for sleeping with other men, perhaps in the fertility rites of the shrines, and that the command is meant to shock. Others note that the Hebrew says a wife of harlotries, not the ordinary word for a prostitute, and think she was faithful when Hosea married her and is named for what she became, as Israel was faithful in her youth (2:15). Still others, some medieval Jewish interpreters among them, read the marriage as a vision or a parable, though most modern scholars think the names of Gomer and her father point to a real marriage.

On any reading, Hosea's pain mirrors God's. The names of the children carry the message. Jezreel recalls the place where Jehu wiped out the house of Ahab (2 Kings 9 to 10), and announces the end of Jehu's line. Lo-ruhamah means No Compassion. Lo-ammi means Not My People, the covenant words of Sinai spoken in reverse. Then, before the chapter ends, every name is turned inside out. In the very place where they were called Not My People, they will be called sons of the living God (1:10).

In chapter 3 the LORD says, ‘Go show love to your wife again’ (3:1). Hosea buys her back for silver and barley and sets a time of waiting, as Israel must live many days without king or sacrifice before it returns ‘and seek the LORD their God and David their king’ (3:5). Most readers take her to be Gomer, and the story to be the love that goes after the one who left.

This is a prophetic sign, one man's life carrying God's grief for a nation. It is not a model for anyone's marriage, and it gives no warrant for any man to shame or harm a wife.

Chapter 2 is a lawsuit. The LORD speaks as a wronged husband, and the wife is Israel as a people. She has gone after her lovers, Baal and the powers she trusted, and has said that they gave her bread and water, wool and linen. She does not acknowledge that ‘it was I who gave her grain, new wine, and oil’ (2:8).

Then come the hardest lines in the book. Verses 3 and 10 threaten to strip the wife and expose her. Many readers find these lines painful, and readers who have known abuse may find them very hard. The site's notes give several things that help. The chapter is a picture of a nation, and the stripping describes what invasion and famine would do to a land, left bare like a desert. The images come from the legal customs of the ancient world, which prophets used to make the weight of covenant betrayal felt. Scholars weigh the problem differently. Some, many feminist interpreters among them, argue that the picture has shaped harmful attitudes and must be read critically. Others stress that it describes God's judgment on a nation and never permits any husband to act this way. Both agree that using it to justify the mistreatment of women is a grave misuse.

So it must be said plainly. These verses are a prophetic picture of God and a nation. They give no warrant for any man to shame, strip, threaten or harm a wife, or anyone.

Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line. These notes are not legal advice. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

And the chapter does not end in the courtroom. ‘Therefore, behold, I will allure her and lead her to the wilderness, and speak to her tenderly’ (2:14). The Valley of Achor, a name that recalled trouble, becomes ‘a gateway of hope’ (2:15). She will call him her husband, not her master (2:16), since the word baal could mean master or husband, and the names of the Baals will be forgotten. ‘So I will betroth you to Me forever; I will betroth you in righteousness and justice, in loving devotion and compassion’ (2:19). The names of chapter 1 are reversed. God will have compassion on No Compassion, and say to Not My People that they are his people (2:23).

parts.h: No knowledge of God in the land
parts.body:
Chapter 4 opens the second half with another lawsuit. ‘There is no truth, no loving devotion, and no knowledge of God in the land’ (4:1). To know God, in Hosea, is not to hold information about him. It is the close, loyal knowing of a covenant partner, the kind of knowing that marriage also names.

The priests bear the heaviest blame. ‘My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge’ (4:6), because the priests have rejected the law they were meant to teach. The people consult wooden idols and go to the hilltop shrines, where worship has become sexual immorality. Bethel, the house of God, Hosea calls Beth-aven, house of wickedness (4:15).

Chapter 6 shows how shallow repentance can be. The people sing, ‘Come, let us return to the LORD’ (6:1), sure that the God who tore them will heal them, ‘on the third day He will raise us up’ (6:2). God answers with grief: ‘your loyalty is like a morning mist, like the early dew that vanishes’ (6:4). Then comes the verse Jesus quoted twice: ‘For I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings’ (6:6).

Hosea's word for that loyalty is hesed, rendered in the BSB as loving devotion or loyalty. It is the faithfulness covenant partners owe each other. God has shown it to Israel from the exodus. He wants it from them more than any offering.

parts.h: Kings, calves and a senseless dove
parts.body:
Hosea treats Israel's politics as a matter of worship. ‘They set up kings, but not by Me’ (8:4). In the years after Jeroboam II, kings were murdered one after another, and chapter 7 pictures the plotters as an oven, hot all night, that devours its rulers. Ephraim mixes with the nations ‘like a silly, senseless dove’ (7:11), calling to Egypt one year and to Assyria the next.

The calf of Samaria stands at the center of the charge. Jeroboam I had set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan, probably as pedestals or images of the LORD, though the line between the LORD and Baal had blurred. Hosea mocks it: ‘a craftsman made it, and it is not God’ (8:6). It will be carried off to Assyria as tribute (10:5-6). Their verdict is a proverb: ‘For they sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind’ (8:7).

The judgments in these chapters are severe. Hosea speaks of exile, of festivals ended, and of the loss of children (9:11-16). He names the war crimes of his day as crimes and warns that Israel will suffer them (10:14; 13:16). These notes name those verses and do not describe them. They are not a pattern for anyone, and they are no key for reading any people's suffering, then or now, as deserved. This is Israel's own Scripture, and its harshest words are aimed at its own nation. It is never a reason to blame the Jewish people.

Even here the call to return breaks in: ‘Sow for yourselves righteousness and reap the fruit of loving devotion; break up your unplowed ground’ (10:12).

parts.h: The Father who taught his son to walk
parts.body:
Chapter 11 is the heart of the book. The marriage picture gives way to a parent and a child. ‘When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called My son’ (11:1). The more God called, the farther Israel ran to the Baals. Yet ‘It was I who taught Ephraim to walk, taking them in My arms’ (11:3). He led them ‘with cords of kindness, with ropes of love’ and bent down to feed them (11:4).

Judgment by Assyria is coming, and the chapter does not hide it. Then God's own heart turns. ‘How could I give you up, O Ephraim? How could I surrender you, O Israel?’ (11:8). Admah and Zeboiim were cities destroyed with Sodom and Gomorrah, bywords for total ruin. God will not make Ephraim like them. ‘For I am God and not man’ (11:9), the Holy One among them. His holiness is the reason his anger does not have the last word.

The chapter ends with the LORD roaring like a lion and his children coming home trembling from Egypt and Assyria (11:10-11). Hosea, raised in a world where the exodus was the great rescue, already expects God to rescue again.

parts.h: From Jacob to the last call
parts.body:
Chapters 12 to 14 gather the book together. Hosea reaches back to Jacob, the nation's ancestor, who grasped his brother's heel in the womb, wrestled with God, and wept and sought his favor (12:3-4). Ephraim has his ancestor's deceit without his tears. The merchant with dishonest scales boasts that his wealth proves he has done nothing wrong (12:7-8).

Chapter 13 is the darkest. The God who knew Israel in the wilderness will fall on it like a lion, a leopard, and a bear robbed of her cubs (13:7-8), and the kings Israel asked for cannot save it. In the middle of the doom comes a verse read two ways. ‘I will ransom them from the power of Sheol; I will redeem them from Death’ (13:14) may be a promise, or, read as questions in the Hebrew, a threat; the verses around it are judgment. Paul later took up its taunt at death (1 Corinthians 15:55).

Then the last chapter gives the people the words to come home. ‘Take away all our iniquity and receive us graciously’ (14:2). They renounce trust in Assyria, horses and idols: ‘For in You the fatherless find compassion’ (14:3). God answers, ‘I will heal their apostasy; I will freely love them, for My anger has turned away from them’ (14:4). He pictures Israel blossoming like a lily and rooted like the cedars of Lebanon. The last verse speaks to every later reader: ‘Whoever is wise, let him understand these things’ (14:9).

parts.h: How the New Testament reads Hosea
parts.body:
The New Testament quotes Hosea several times, and these notes draw only the lines it draws. Jesus twice used 6:6 against religion without mercy: ‘But go and learn what this means’ (Matthew 9:13), and again when his disciples were condemned for picking grain on the Sabbath (Matthew 12:7).

Matthew tells of the child Jesus brought back from Egypt and says it fulfilled what the Lord had spoken through the prophet (Matthew 2:15), quoting 11:1. Hosea was speaking of the exodus, and Matthew knew it. Many interpreters call his reading typological: Jesus, the Son in a unique sense, lives through Israel's story faithfully. Others point out that Hosea himself expected a new exodus (11:10-11). Either way, Matthew does not claim that Hosea foresaw Jesus' childhood. He claims that Jesus completes the story Hosea told.

Paul quotes the reversal of the names to show God's mercy reaching Gentiles as well as Jews: ‘As He says in Hosea’ (Romans 9:25), and Peter writes, ‘Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God’ (1 Peter 2:10). Paul turns 13:14 into a song of resurrection: ‘Where, O Death, is your victory? Where, O Death, is your sting?’ (1 Corinthians 15:55). Jesus, on the way to the cross, used the words of 10:8 about people who will say to the mountains, ‘Fall on us’ (Luke 23:30).

Many Christians hear 6:2, ‘on the third day He will raise us up’, behind the confession that Christ was raised on the third day, but the New Testament never quotes the verse. These notes leave that reading as a reading. Hosea's warnings were spoken to Israel by an Israelite prophet, and the New Testament never uses them to blame the Jewish people.

Read Hosea a few verses at a time, and notice who is speaking. The voice moves between the LORD, the prophet and the people, sometimes inside one verse. Let the pictures do their work: a half-baked cake, a senseless dove, a morning mist, a stubborn heifer, a lion, a moth, a lily.

Read the marriage chapters with care. The picture uses the world of ancient Israel, where a husband held legal authority over his wife, and some of its images of punishment are harsh. It describes God and a nation. It is not a model for any human marriage, and it has been wrongly used to excuse the abuse of women. Watch where it goes: every speech of judgment in chapters 1 to 3 ends in renewal.

Read the judgments as Israel's own Scripture, spoken by one of its own prophets to his own people. They are a warning to take to oneself, not a verdict to pronounce on anyone else's suffering. And read to the end. The book's last word to Israel is not the sword but the invitation of 14:1, ‘Return, O Israel, to the LORD your God’, and the promise to heal and love freely.

hard.line: God tells Hosea to marry ‘a prostitute’: three readings of who Gomer was.
Jezreel: judgment on Jehu's house for a purge that 2 Kings 10:30 credits to God's word.
The threats to strip and expose the unfaithful wife: a picture of a nation, never a warrant to shame or harm a wife.
Hosea buys back his wife and sets a time of waiting: is she Gomer, and why must she wait?
God will not punish the daughters for adultery: the blame laid on the men and the priests.
God as a moth, as rot, and as a lion tearing its prey.
The people's song of return, and whether the third day points to Jesus.
The calf of Samaria: an image of the LORD or of another god?
The prophet's prayer that Ephraim have no children: named, not lingered on.
Mothers and children in war: an atrocity named as a crime, not described.
‘Out of Egypt I called My son’: how Matthew can say a verse about the exodus was fulfilled.
God's heart turns, and he will not destroy Ephraim completely.
A promise of rescue from death, or a threat: the Hebrew read two ways.
Samaria's fall by the sword: the cruelty of war named, not described.

words.line: Loving devotion or loyalty: the faithful love covenant partners owe each other. God desires it more than sacrifice (6:6) and will betroth his people in it (2:19).
Not information but the loyal, close knowing of a covenant partner. Its lack is the root of Israel's sin (4:1, 6).
To act as a prostitute: the book's main picture of Israel's unfaithfulness, from the wife of harlotries (1:2) onward.
The storm and fertility god of Canaan, credited with rain and harvest. The word also meant master or husband, which is why 2:16 sets it aside.
‘God sows’: a city and valley where Jehu shed blood, and in the end the name of a great day of planting (1:4, 11; 2:22).
‘No Compassion’, Hosea's daughter. The word comes from the word for womb. God will have compassion on her (2:23).
‘Not My People’, Hosea's second son: the covenant words spoken in reverse, and then reversed again (1:9-10; 2:23).
The largest northern tribe, and Hosea's usual name for the whole northern kingdom (5:3; 11:8).
House of wickedness: Hosea's mocking name for Bethel, the house of God, where the calf stood (4:15; 10:5).
The calf image set up by Jeroboam I and still worshiped, which ‘a craftsman made’ (8:5-6; 10:5).
To turn or return. Israel will not return to God, so it will return to a new Egypt; yet the book ends with ‘Return, O Israel’ (14:1).
The bond between the LORD and Israel, here pictured as a marriage. Israel has broken it (6:7; 8:1), and God promises a new one (2:18).
The realm of the dead. God speaks of ransoming his people from it, or of summoning its plagues (13:14).

timeline.what: The kingdom divides. Jeroboam I becomes king of the north and sets up golden calves at Bethel and Dan (1 Kings 12).
Jehu kills Joram, Ahaziah, Jezebel and Ahab's house at Jezreel (2 Kings 9 to 10): ‘the bloodshed of Jezreel’ of 1:4.
Jeroboam II reigns in Israel, a time of wider borders and wealth. Hosea begins in his reign (1:1).
Amos, a man from Judah, preaches at Bethel under Jeroboam II.
Hosea begins to preach. The site's guide to the kings has him speaking to about 715 BC; the book's introduction gives about 755 to about 725.
Jeroboam's son Zechariah reigns six months and is murdered. Jehu's line ends, as 1:4 warned (2 Kings 15:8-12).
Menahem reigns and pays Assyria a heavy tribute (2 Kings 15:19-20).
Tiglath-pileser III begins to rule Assyria and turns west.
Israel and Damascus fight Judah and Assyria. Many scholars connect 5:8-15 with this war. Galilee and Gilead are lost.
Hoshea, the last king of Israel, comes to the throne. He later stops paying tribute and turns to Egypt (2 Kings 17:4).
Samaria falls after a three-year siege, and much of its people is deported (2 Kings 17:5-6). The guide to the kings, following Thiele, gives 723 or 722.
Hezekiah becomes king of Judah, the last king named in Hosea's heading (1:1).
Hosea's words are carried south and kept in Judah, where most scholars think the book took its final form.

map.title: The northern kingdom in Hosea's day

places.name: Samaria
places.line: The northern capital and its hill country. Its calf is rejected (8:5), and it will fall by the sword (13:16). Drawn roughly, as a region; the city is not marked.

places.name: Bethel
places.line: Where Jacob met God (12:4), and where Jeroboam's calf stood. Hosea calls it Beth-aven, house of wickedness (4:15; 10:5).

places.name: Shechem
places.line: Priests lie in ambush on the road to Shechem (6:9).

places.name: Gilead
places.line: The land east of the Jordan, ‘a city of evildoers’ (6:8), lost to Assyria in Hosea's day. Drawn roughly, as a region.

teaching.mapNote: Only four places are drawn, each at a point already used on this site's maps; Samaria and Gilead roughly, as regions. Jezreel, Gilgal, Gibeah, Ramah, Mizpah, Tabor, Adam, the Valley of Achor, Admah and Zeboiim, and Lebanon are left off, because they are not placed in this site's records, and so are Egypt and Assyria. No borders are drawn. The map makes no claim about any border today.
